title: Frighteningly Ambitious Startup Ideas: why the biggest ideas repel you and how to start small
summary: Graham argues the biggest startup ideas feel frightening, so most idea-hunters filter them out subconsciously. He sketches seven examples, then gives tactics: don't announce the giant goal, start with something deceptively small, and head "westward" like Columbus rather than plotting a precise future.

principles.text: The biggest startup ideas feel scary and threaten your identity, so your subconscious filters them out; approach them obliquely.
principles.quote: You'd expect big startup ideas to be attractive, but actually they tend to repel you. And that has a bunch of consequences. It means these ideas are invisible to most people who try to think of startup ideas, because their subconscious filters them out.

principles.text: Win a market by first owning a small, intensely loyal core of users, even if it constrains you later.
principles.quote: Don't worry if something you want to do will constrain you in the long term, because if you don't get that initial core of users, there won't be a long term.

principles.text: Build what you yourself want; if you are the target user, the route to the first users is straightforward.
principles.quote: Since anyone capable of starting this company is one of those 10,000 hackers, the route is at least straightforward: make the search engine you yourself want.

principles.text: Don't announce the giant ambition; describe it as something harmless to avoid inflated expectations and haters.
principles.quote: Don't say, for example, that you're going to replace email. If you do that you raise too many expectations. Your employees and investors will constantly be asking "are we there yet?" and you'll have an army of haters waiting to see you fail.

principles.text: Really big companies start from deceptively small things, and founders themselves should start small.
principles.quote: Empirically, the way to do really big things seems to be to start with deceptively small things.

principles.text: Head in a general direction like Columbus instead of building toward a precise vision of the future; a blurry view may be better.
principles.quote: The popular image of the visionary is someone with a clear view of the future, but empirically it may be better to have a blurry one.
